o: For each drone compute Manhattan distance |x-tx| + |y-ty|; keep the best (smallest distance, ties broken by smaller index) among drones whose distance is within their range. With at most 100 drones, one straightforward pass is optimal. Example 2 shows tie-breaking: drones 1 and 2 both at distance 2, so we return 1.
k: Manhattan distance is computed directly; no geometry tricks needed.
Track (distance, index) lexicographically: strictly smaller distance wins, otherwise keep the earlier index.
Filter by range before comparing candidates.

a.n: Approach 1: Single Pass Tracking Best Candidate
a.i: Iterate drones in index order; compute distance; if within range and strictly better than the current best distance, update best index. Scanning in increasing index order makes strict inequality sufficient for tie-breaking by smallest index.
s: For each drone i: compute d = |x-tx| + |y-ty|; if d <= range and d < bestDist, set bestDist = d, bestIdx = i.
a.t: O(m) — one pass over m drones with constant work each.

w: This linear scan is already optimal; a second approach would add nothing. Pitfalls: using strict '<=' against bestD (breaks tie-breaking toward the smaller index), checking range after updating best, and off-by-one on 'less than or equal to range'. Edge cases: no reachable drone returns -1; a drone exactly at range boundary is reachable. Follow-ups: nearest by Euclidean distance, or range queries over many targets (would need spatial indexing).
